title_en: How a Chicago Restaurant Has Stayed Open For Nearly Three Decades
title_zh: 一家芝加哥餐厅如何开了近三十年
subtitle_zh: Odd Lots 走进芝加哥：North Pond 餐厅与 Spark 共享厨房的老板 Richard Mott 讲述高级餐饮残酷的经济学、'从农场到餐桌'的兴起，以及为何套餐越来越贵、酒却越卖越少。
summary_zh: 本期在 Chicago 现场录制的 Odd Lots 中，Tracy Alloway 与 Joe Weisenthal 请来本地 North Pond 餐厅与 Spark 共享厨房（Spark Shared Kitchen）的老板 Richard Mott——他曾在 University of Chicago 的 Booth 商学院主修金融，却在 Progressive Insurance 实习三个月后决意不再为任何人打工、转而创业。主持人指出，餐饮之所以迷人，是因为它像「巨无霸指数」（Big Mac Index）一样嵌入了劳动力、大宗商品成本与租金等经济中的每一项投入。Mott 复盘 1980 年代接手 North Pond 的往事：那片林肯公园角落当时还是流浪汉聚集、池塘形同郊区排水沟的荒废之地，因无人竞标才拿到合同，起初只能以「North Pond Cafe」的休闲形态开业、甚至不许设吧台，直到有远见的公园管理者批准改造升级。他剖析高级餐饮（fine dining）残酷的经济学：这门生意几乎没有进入壁垒、难以建起护城河（moat），你发明的「牛角甜甜圈」（croissant donut）全世界都能复制；一份 130 美元的五道菜套餐背后是厨房与甜点部门九到十人的投入，而平均每瓶约 110 美元的葡萄酒利润率相当、却几乎不需要对应成本，正因如此酒卖得越来越少让老板们紧张。他还谈到 North Pond 日益成为「人生特别事件」的体验型消费，以及 Spark 共享厨房如何汇集资本、租约与执照，让擅长风味的厨师不必自购两万美元的冰淇淋机——是一集透过餐饮看宏观经济与创业的实操深谈。

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios Podcasts Radio News.
turns.zh: 彭博音频工作室（Bloomberg Audio Studios），播客、广播、新闻。

turns.en: Music Hello and welcome to another episode of the OddLots Podcast. I'm Traci Alloway.
turns.zh: （音乐）大家好，欢迎收听新一期的 Odd Lots 播客。我是崔西·阿洛威（Tracy Alloway）。

turns.en: And I'm Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: 我是乔·魏森塔尔（Joe Weisenthal）。

turns.en: Joe, we are back in Chicago.
turns.zh: 乔，我们又回到芝加哥了。

turns.en: I love Chicago.
turns.zh: 我爱芝加哥。

turns.en: It's a beautiful city. I used to live here. It's always kind of surreal coming back because it reminds me of middle school, basically. We're actually here for a live show, but I thought we would squeeze in one additional episode. It's one of the kind of favorite types of episodes that we like to do.
turns.zh: 这是座美丽的城市。我以前就住在这儿。每次回来都有点恍如隔世，因为它基本上会让我想起读中学的时候。我们这次其实是来做一场现场演出的，但我想我们可以额外再塞进一期节目。这是我们最喜欢做的那类节目之一。

turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.en: It's a food service. episode, one of our favorite genres of episodes. One of our favorite episodes we ever did was a Chicago-based food service entity, The Baker.
turns.zh: 这是一期餐饮服务业（food service）的节目，是我们最喜欢的题材之一。我们做过的最喜欢的一期，讲的就是一家总部在芝加哥的餐饮服务商——那位烘焙师傅（The Baker）。

turns.en: Remember him?
turns.zh: 还记得他吗？

turns.en: Absolutely. And one of the reasons these episodes are so interesting to do is, you know, we have a lot of economists on the show. We have a lot of investors, whoever. And they kind of talk about business in this conceptual way. But it's always interesting talking to actual practitioners in the space. And the thing about food is it touches on so many different aspects of the macro economy. You know, you have labor, you have supply chain issues, you have general, I guess, entrepreneurial issues as well. And so I thought we would talk to someone a little bit different to the Chicago-based baker. We would talk to someone who not only comes from, I guess, sort of a finance background, but someone who actually left finance at an undergraduate level in order, he made the conscious decision to become a practitioner in the restaurant and catering space.
turns.zh: 当然记得。这类节目之所以这么有意思，一个原因是，你知道，我们节目请过很多经济学家，请过很多投资人等等各种人。他们谈论商业时往往是从概念层面切入的。但和真正在这个领域里实操的人聊天总是很有意思。而食物这件事，它触及宏观经济的方方面面。比如劳动力、供应链问题，我想还有普遍的创业问题。所以我想我们这次要找一位和那位芝加哥烘焙师傅稍微不同的人。我们要找的这个人，不仅算是金融背景出身，而且是在本科阶段就主动离开了金融——他有意识地决定投身餐厅和宴会承办（catering）这一行，成为一名实操者。

turns.en: You know, the Big Mac index, right? Yeah, of course.
turns.zh: 你知道的，就像巨无霸指数（Big Mac Index），对吧？是啊，当然。

turns.en: The reason why that works as a concept is because embedded within the Big Mac is labor, commodity costs and rent.
turns.zh: 巨无霸指数之所以能作为一个概念成立，是因为一个巨无霸里就嵌入了劳动力、大宗商品成本和租金。

turns.en: And that's everything, right?
turns.zh: 而这些就是一切了，对吧？

turns.en: And so here you get the reason why these particular businesses are so fascinating to us is because, as you said, every input goes into it. Every input in the economy goes into it in some way. And then, of course, the chance to someone who sort of knows business both from a theoretical background and also a entrepreneurial background That's a good guest.
turns.zh: 所以这也正是为什么这类特定的生意对我们如此有吸引力——就像你说的，每一种投入都要用到它上面。经济中的每一项投入，都会以某种方式进入这门生意。而且，当然，能请到一位既从理论背景、又从创业背景两方面都懂商业的人，那可是一位好嘉宾。

turns.en: And someone who's had experience running different types of food businesses. So this will be really interesting. I'm very happy to say we have the perfect guest. We're going to be speaking with Richard Mott. He is the owner of North Pond here in Chicago. He is also the owner of the Spark Shared Kitchen, which we'll get into exactly what that is. And he studied finance at the University of Chicago. So truly the perfect guest. Richard, thank you so much for coming on.
turns.zh: 而且还是一位有过经营多种不同类型餐饮生意经验的人。所以这会非常有意思。我很高兴地说，我们请到了完美的嘉宾。我们今天要与理查德·莫特（Richard Mott）对话。他是芝加哥本地 North Pond 餐厅的老板，同时也是 Spark 共享厨房（Spark Shared Kitchen）的老板——待会儿我们会详细讲讲那到底是什么。他曾在芝加哥大学（University of Chicago）学习金融。所以真是一位完美的嘉宾。理查德，非常感谢你来做客。

turns.en: Oh, thank you for having me. I'm glad to be here.
turns.zh: 哦，谢谢你们邀请我。很高兴来到这里。

turns.en: So I mentioned finance was your undergraduate expertise, but I also said you made a decision that you didn't want to stay in finance. Talk to us about how you actually got into the restaurant business.
turns.zh: 我刚才提到金融是你本科阶段的专业方向，但我也说了你后来决定不想再留在金融界。跟我们讲讲你是怎么真正进入餐饮业的吧。

turns.en: Well, actually, I was a history, urban studies, political science major as an undergrad at the University of Buffalo. But I attended Booth, the graduate school at the University of Chicago, where I was a finance major. And I did my internship there. I did in the finance department of Progressive Insurance, which at the time was sort of a young, fast-moving upstart. I mean, it was a great company to work for and everything. But I left that summer with just the realization I really didn't want to work for anyone else, and I wanted to start a venture of my own. So three months in a corporate office was enough to kick me out of that field for the rest of my life.
turns.zh: 其实，我本科在布法罗大学（University of Buffalo）主修的是历史、城市研究和政治学。但我读了芝加哥大学的研究生院布斯商学院（Booth），在那里我主修金融。我的实习也是在那期间做的，是在前进保险公司（Progressive Insurance）的财务部门，那家公司当时算是个年轻、动作飞快、正在崛起的新秀。我的意思是，那是家很棒的公司，什么都好。但那个夏天结束离开时，我意识到自己真的不想再为任何人打工，我想创办属于自己的事业。所以在公司办公室里待了三个月，就足以把我这辈子都踢出那个行业了。

turns.en: These days, if you were to like go to Stanford Business School or at Wharton for sure, you would find tons of people who are there because they want to be entrepreneurs or maybe they want to be VCs or they want to have a so-called like search fund where they gather a couple million dollars from their friends and buy some local pool repair companies or whatever.
turns.zh: 如今，如果你去斯坦福商学院（Stanford Business School），或者尤其是沃顿商学院（Wharton），你会发现一大把人读商学院是因为他们想创业，或者想当风险投资人（VC），又或者想搞一个所谓的“搜索基金”（search fund）——就是从朋友那里募集几百万美元，然后买下某家本地的泳池维修公司之类的。

turns.en: And But I guess like that's sort of novel.
turns.zh: 不过我想那种做法算是比较新潮的。

turns.en: And I guess like in the past, like someone who was at these schools, it was just purely a pipeline for working at a big firm.
turns.zh: 我想在过去，读这些学校的人，纯粹就是把学校当成进入大公司工作的一条流水线。

turns.en: It's very complete, 180 degree sea change on this. When I was at school, there was no such thing as entrepreneurial studies. There were no seminars on small business financing. There was absolutely nothing paid attention to any of those fields. You were being trained to work for Continental Bank. for Citicorp, for McKinsey, those types of companies. And my decision to go off on my own and start a business, which I had started my second year of business school, was sort of met with a lot of bewilderment by some of my classmates. And even to the point where some were kind of derisively asking questions like, oh, what's the matter, Rich? Didn't you get a real job offer? That kind of thing. And the really ironic thing is that now, at Booth, the largest single concentration, larger than marketing or finance, the largest single concentration at the school right now is entrepreneurial studies. And it is a huge part of the business. And they've also spun off from that the Polsky Center, which is the university-wide center for entrepreneurship and monetizing advances in their physics labs and things like that. But It is a very big and very successful part of the university now. And if you go to all the top business schools, you go to the Whartons, the Harvards, the Stanford, Berkeley, they all have very, very dynamic spaces, entrepreneurial spaces, and labs, classes. It's an incredibly supportive environment right now.
turns.zh: 在这方面已经发生了彻底的、一百八十度的巨变。我上学那会儿，根本没有“创业研究”这回事。没有关于小企业融资的研讨课。完全没有任何人关注那些领域。你受到的训练就是去大陆银行（Continental Bank）、花旗集团（Citicorp）、麦肯锡（McKinsey）那类公司工作。而我决定自己单干、去创业——我在商学院第二年就创办了自己的公司——这在我一些同学看来简直莫名其妙。甚至有人带着嘲讽的口气问：哦，怎么了，里奇（Rich）？你没拿到正经的工作 offer 吗？诸如此类。而真正讽刺的是，如今在布斯商学院，人数最多的单一专业方向，比市场营销或金融都多，现在学校里人数最多的单一方向就是创业研究。它已经成为商学院极其重要的一部分。他们还由此衍生出了波尔斯基中心（Polsky Center），那是全校性的创业中心，负责把物理实验室之类的科研进展商业化变现。它如今是这所大学里非常庞大且非常成功的一部分。如果你去所有顶尖商学院——沃顿、哈佛、斯坦福、伯克利——它们都有非常非常有活力的创业空间、实验室和课程。当下那是一个支持力度极强的环境。

turns.en: That's such an interesting shift. But when you were at grad school, I think I read that you bid on a school project to actually start a coffee shop.
turns.zh: 这个转变真有意思。不过你读研究生那会儿，我记得我读到过，你竞标了一个学校的项目，真的去开了一家咖啡店。

turns.en: They had a coffee shop in the basement of the business school, and they would let a couple students run it every year. And I bid on it and turned it from a coffee shop into, you know, let's get bagels, let's get sandwiches. Pretty soon we got a whole little lunchroom there. Turned out to be quite a successful little venture. I got approached by a couple other departments of the school. So one thing led to another. And by the time I graduated, we had four locations on campus and started this as a full-time business. And by, you know, eight, nine years later, we had a chain of 20 of these. And they were all coffee slash sandwich shops, but they were all in the academic buildings. So we didn't do the main board plans, you know, with Compass and Aramark typically do. We were just doing the small little almost bespoke operations within the academic buildings.
turns.zh: 商学院的地下室里有一家咖啡店，学校每年会让几个学生来经营它。我把它竞标了下来，然后把它从一家咖啡店变成了——你懂的，我们上贝果吧，我们上三明治吧。很快我们就在那里搞出了一个完整的小午餐室。结果成了相当成功的一桩小生意。学校里另外几个院系也来找我谈。于是一件事接着一件事。到我毕业的时候，我们在校园里已经开了四个点，并把它当成一份全职生意来做。大概又过了八九年，我们已经拥有了一条由 20 家这样的店组成的连锁。它们全都是咖啡兼三明治店，但都开在教学楼里。所以我们不做那种大型食堂承包方案——你知道的，就是康帕斯（Compass）和雅玛客（Aramark）通常做的那种。我们只做教学楼里那种小而近乎定制化（bespoke）的经营。

turns.en: Did you get to keep the profit from the coffee shops?
turns.zh: 那些咖啡店的利润你能自己留下吗？

turns.en: Yes, that was a complete P & L. We paid them a rent and it worked out very well for us because we'd reached an agreement on the rent based on basically just being a coffee shop and then kind of quadrupling the revenue and turning it into a real sort of lunchroom made it And for an undergrad, more money than I'd ever seen in my life. I mean, that wasn't a lot of money, but still.
turns.zh: 能，那是一份完整的损益表（P&L）。我们付租金给学校，而这对我们非常划算，因为我们当初谈租金时基本上是按“就是一家咖啡店”来定的，后来我们把营收做到了差不多四倍，把它变成了一个真正意义上的午餐室。对一个本科生来说，那是我这辈子见过最多的钱。我的意思是，那其实不算一大笔钱，但无论如何也够可观了。

turns.en: You know, it's funny because we're like talking about the evolution of business schools. And that's maybe a lens through which to understand the history of the American economy. You could tell probably the history of the American economy through coffee shops themselves. And you think about like first generation coffee shops and then the Starbucks's. And then now like the explosion of like, oh, you have to have, with pistachio syrup and all these things.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，我们正在聊商学院的演变。而这也许是理解美国经济史的一个视角。你其实很可能能通过咖啡店本身来讲出美国经济的历史。你会想到第一代咖啡店，然后是星巴克（Starbucks）这类，再到如今的爆发——哦，你必须得来一杯加了开心果糖浆之类各种配料的东西。

turns.en: I had a pumpkin matcha cream latte this morning. Don't judge me.
turns.zh: 我今天早上喝了一杯南瓜抹茶奶油拿铁。别笑话我。

turns.en: I don't normally get those.
turns.zh: 我平常不会点那种。

turns.en: There's about too, too many ingredients in.
turns.zh: 那里面放的配料实在太多了。

turns.en: That one right there.
turns.zh: 就是说那一杯。

turns.en: Well, I never drink that stuff. But the other day I was walking home and I saw this. It was like a banana pudding flavored latte with cardamom.
turns.zh: 嗯，我从来不喝那种东西。但前几天我走路回家时看到了一个，是一杯香蕉布丁味、还加了小豆蔻（cardamom）的拿铁。

turns.en: And those are like, I was so tempted.
turns.zh: 那种东西嘛，我当时真的好心动。

turns.en: I wish I could say that sounds bad to me, but it sounds fantastic.
turns.zh: 真希望我能说那听起来很难喝，但它听起来太棒了。

turns.en: I know, I was so tempted, but it's like, I can't do it.
turns.zh: 我知道，我真的好心动，但就是——我下不了手。

turns.en: But actually, I am curious, like, What years were this? And what were you serving? What was a coffee shop expected to have in those years?
turns.zh: 不过其实我很好奇，那是什么年代的事？你们当时卖些什么？那些年人们觉得一家咖啡店应该有些什么？

turns.en: Coffee was a very, very different industry. I mean, we served coffee, soda. We didn't serve water. There wasn't any bottled water back then. It was coffee and soda, sandwiches, soup, a lot of pastries and baked goods.
turns.zh: 咖啡那时是一个完全完全不同的行业。我的意思是，我们卖咖啡、卖汽水。我们不卖水。那时候根本没有瓶装水。就是咖啡和汽水、三明治、汤，还有大量的糕点和烘焙食品。

turns.en: And by coffee, that was just like a cap or decaf?
turns.zh: 你说的咖啡，就是那种普通咖啡（regular）或者低咖啡因（decaf）吗？

turns.en: This was the old one you would have gotten in the, you know, where you would have gotten in a marine barracks with the big bun, three-gallon pour-over thing. And I'm... I'm not a real coffee drinker, but if you were to go back and taste it now, I'm sure it would be just wretched.
turns.zh: 就是那种老式的咖啡，你知道的，就是你在海军陆战队营房里会喝到的那种，用一个大大的滤泡壶、三加仑容量的手冲壶煮出来的。我……我并不是个真正喝咖啡的人，但如果你现在回去尝尝那种咖啡，我保证它会难喝得可怕。

turns.en: No, I love that stuff. I'm fine with industrial grade coffee.
turns.zh: 不，我就爱那种。工业级咖啡我也能接受。

turns.en: Well, the other thing that's kind of funny is we served coffee. We had two sizes of coffees. We had a seven ounce, that was our small, and a 10 ounce, which was the large coffee. And now if you go to a coffee shop, most smalls are larger than the large that we had at that time. And don't claim any great foresight in that you know, back then in the coffee market. I remember my wife came back, Starbucks, Chicago was the first city outside of the Northwest that they'd opened in. And my wife, who's a coffee addict, came back and said she went to this great store, they had coffee, and that was pretty much all they served, but it was great coffee and great service and everything. And I just poo-pooed the whole thing. I was like, oh, a store that just serves coffee, yeah, how long is that going to last? And then I end up opening 20 coffee shops.
turns.zh: 另一件挺好玩的事是，我们卖咖啡，我们有两种杯型。我们有 7 盎司的，那是我们的小杯，还有 10 盎司的，那是大杯。而现在你去咖啡店，大多数店的小杯都比我们那时候的大杯还要大。不过可别把这当成我在咖啡市场上有什么了不起的远见。我记得我太太从……星巴克——芝加哥是它在美国西北地区以外开设门店的第一座城市——我太太是个咖啡上瘾者，她回来说她去了这家很棒的店，他们卖咖啡，而且基本上只卖咖啡，但那咖啡非常好，服务也一流，等等。我却对这整件事嗤之以鼻。我心想：哦，一家只卖咖啡的店，能开多久啊？结果最后我自己开了 20 家咖啡店。

turns.en: What was the most challenging aspect of running that type of coffee shop business at the time?
turns.zh: 在当时经营那种咖啡店生意，最有挑战性的方面是什么？

turns.en: By the way, what years are we talking about?
turns.zh: 顺便问一下，我们说的是哪几年？

turns.en: Oh, I graduated in 82. So I started this in 1981. So yeah, the very, I think Starbucks might have come to Chicago mid 80s, 86, maybe 87, somewhere around in there. So this was still, you bought the coffee, you bought it in five-pound bags, and you scooped it out, and that coffee could be sitting around. If you didn't use it at the end of June when glasses closed, you just put it in a container and use it in September. I mean, the kind of things that would get you shot by a coffee lover these days. So it was a hot brown beverage is what it was.
turns.zh: 哦，我是 1982 年毕业的。所以我是 1981 年开始做这个的。所以是的，很早——我想星巴克大概是 80 年代中期到的芝加哥，86 年，也许 87 年，大概在那前后。所以那时候还是这样：你去买咖啡，成袋买，五磅一袋，然后用勺子舀出来，那些咖啡可能就那么放着。如果到了六月底学校放假你还没用完，你就把它装进一个容器里，等到九月接着用。我的意思是，那种做法要是搁到现在，会被咖啡爱好者一枪毙了。所以那时候的咖啡说白了就是一种热的棕色饮料。

turns.en: And the biggest challenge at that time, what was hardest?
turns.zh: 那当时最大的挑战是什么？什么最难？

turns.en: Well, the hardest for me is that I had started this business with absolutely no idea what I was doing. If I were to ever counsel someone about this, I'd go work for someone else, learn the business, and have them pay for your mistakes. I was a little too insistent on working for myself at that time, opened the business, and literally made every mistake you possibly could. Because I had no reference set. I had no peers to go to, no... I was just making everything up as I went.
turns.zh: 对我来说最难的是，我创办这门生意时对自己在干什么毫无概念。如果让我给谁提建议，我会说：先去给别人打工，学会这门生意，让别人来为你的错误买单。我当时太执着于要为自己工作了，于是开了这家公司，结果字面意义上把你能犯的每一个错误都犯了个遍。因为我没有任何参照系，没有可以求教的同行，没有……我完全是一边干一边瞎编。

turns.en: Let's hear some mistakes.
turns.zh: 那说来听听，讲讲这些错误吧。

turns.en: Oh, I got into bad leases. Oh, boy. Hiring people. I think that was probably the biggest thing was hiring people. It took a long time to really figure out how to hire people for the business, not hire them because you like them, that kind of thing. So personnel was probably the biggest problem I overcame. And now you go to business school and hiring and interviewing skills. They're taught in the school, and these things were never taught. Ours, going back to the school question and the differences between now and then, back then, the MBA program, and I only speak from the University of Chicago's viewpoint, it was a very rigorous program, very, very academic focused. There was little There was no emphasis on any of the sort of soft skills of business, public speaking, interviewing people, things like this. It was just a large classroom exercise. And they have completely gotten off of that. Their program now is a very holistic approach to educating someone to run a business. And they have this entire environment. environment to support people who are doing the search funds or doing the entrepreneurship through acquisition. So it's a very, very different atmosphere. And if you were to ask me 15 years ago, before I started working a lot with these entrepreneurial startup companies, you know, my take would be, oh, it's the success. It's 80%. It's the business idea. And I would flip that on the, I said now, and I would say it's 20% and the idea is it's the team and it's the, your environment and it's your support network. Those are the things that make it successful. You know, not the business side. I'd rather, uh, and, and a great example. Um, you know, if we get back, we talk about home chef. When I was approached by Pat, I thought it was a horrible idea. You know, you get a meal kit, you're going to buy food online and they're going to ship it. This is ridiculous. But I absolutely love this young man. And, um, it worked out. I mean, he had an incredibly successful run, you know, starting that company.
turns.zh: 哦，我签过糟糕的租约。天哪。招人——我想那大概是最要命的一件事。我花了很长时间才真正搞明白怎么为生意招人，而不是因为你喜欢某个人就雇他，诸如此类。所以人事问题可能是我克服掉的最大难题。而现在你去商学院，招聘和面试技巧是学校里教的内容，可这些东西过去从来不教。回到刚才那个关于学校、关于今昔差异的话题——那时候的 MBA 项目，我只从芝加哥大学的角度来说，是一个非常严谨、非常非常偏学术的项目。几乎不重视任何商业软技能，比如公开演讲、面试别人这类东西。它就是一场大班授课的演练。而他们现在完全摆脱了那套路子。他们如今的项目采用的是一种非常全面的方式，来培养一个人去经营企业。他们有整整一套环境来支持那些做搜索基金、或者做“通过收购来创业”（entrepreneurship through acquisition）的人。所以那是非常非常不同的氛围。如果你在 15 年前问我——那时我还没开始大量与这些创业型初创公司合作——我的看法会是：哦，成功 80% 靠的是商业点子。而现在我会把这话反过来说：点子只占 20%，真正关键的是团队、是你所处的环境、是你的支持网络。那些才是让企业成功的因素，而不是商业点子本身。我更愿意……举个很好的例子。你知道，如果我们回头再聊，就说 Home Chef（一家送餐食材套装公司）。当帕特（Pat）来找我时，我觉得那是个糟糕透顶的主意。你知道的，一个食材套装（meal kit），你要在网上买食物，然后他们给你寄过来。这太荒唐了。但我特别喜欢这个年轻人。结果呢，事情成了。我的意思是，他在创办那家公司的过程中取得了极其成功的一段历程。

turns.en: Tracy, in the introduction mentioned various endeavors that you've had over time.
turns.zh: 崔西在开场介绍里提到了你这些年来做过的各种事业。

turns.en: What do you give us the.
turns.zh: 你能不能给我们……

turns.en: Sort of broad overview of you're like, footprint, the various, then we can like dive into these things.
turns.zh: 大致讲讲你的整体版图，那些你做过的项目，然后我们再深入聊这些具体的。

turns.en: Your portfolio.
turns.zh: 你的业务组合。

turns.en: Your portfolio of businesses over time so that we can talk about.
turns.zh: 你这些年积累起来的业务组合，这样我们就能聊开。

turns.en: So I started the coffee shop business and grew that over the years. And we're dealing exclusively with academic locations for small coffee shops. And we had a portfolio of 23 shops and we had five universities that we worked for. Unfortunately, we were sort of swimming upstream in terms of the, you know, the food service market. That was about the beginning of the sort of comprehensive contract model with the universities. So they were going to companies like Aramark and Compass and not signing them just to do the, you know, coffee shop. They're signing them. You're going to run our laundry program. You're going to run our cafeterias. You're going to run our bus program. Stadium concessions. Yeah, you're going to run everything. And we were just a tiny little niche company. So eventually we sort of got swallowed up by that. But started with the coffee shop company. That's a very seasonal business. Yeah. We were looking for something to balance the September to May season. Started doing work with the Chicago Park District and ran a bunch of concessions and things like that. And just through a weird set of circumstances, had the opportunity to bid on a facility. It was the old warming house out in Lincoln Park by the Nature Museum. And I mean, I've had friends ask me now, like, oh, how'd you get that contract? You know, someone in City Hall and stuff. I was like, no, at the time, now it's one of the most beautiful places in Lincoln Park. But at the time, it was a very neglected corner of the park. It was a homeless hangout. There was a lot of prostitution going on in the area. They had not redone the, the pond actually looked like a drain, a suburban drainage ditch at the point. So it really wasn't much of a, we got the contract basically because no one else bid on it. So opened up a fine dining restaurant. And that helped balance. That's a very seasonal business too, but the opposite season from the coffee shop. So there was a nice like a synergy on there. And then also with the coffee shops to sort of broaden our reach and take advantage of some of our facilities, we opened a catering company and a vending company and ran those. And then just as a hobby, I invested in, you know, over the year or the 20 years or so invested in eight or nine other startup businesses. I'm just, you know, friends or an associate starting a business and I'd invest or, you know, be a partner or whatever. But it really was just a hobby.
turns.zh: 我从咖啡店生意起家，这些年把它一点点做大。我们专做学术机构场所里的小咖啡店。我们最多时拥有 23 家店的组合，为五所大学服务。不巧的是，在餐饮服务业市场里，我们差不多是逆流而上。那时正好是高校“综合承包”（comprehensive contract）模式兴起的开端。于是学校去找雅玛客、康帕斯这样的公司，不再只签约让他们做咖啡店，而是签给他们：你要负责运营我们的洗衣项目，你要运营我们的食堂，你要运营我们的班车项目，体育场的特许售卖点……是啊，你要把什么都包下来。而我们只是一家小小的利基公司。所以最终我们差不多被这股浪潮吞没了。但我是从咖啡店公司起家的。那是一门季节性很强的生意。是的。我们想找点东西来平衡九月到五月这个旺季，于是开始和芝加哥公园管理局（Chicago Park District）合作，经营一堆特许售卖点之类的。然后就是机缘巧合，通过一连串奇怪的际遇，我们有机会去竞标一处设施——就是林肯公园（Lincoln Park）里、自然博物馆（Nature Museum）旁边的那座老取暖小屋（warming house）。我是说，现在有朋友问我：哦，你怎么拿到那份合同的？是不是市政府里有人啊之类的。我说：不，那时候——现在它已经是林肯公园里最美的地方之一了，但那时候那是公园里非常被忽视的一个角落。那是流浪汉聚集的地方。那一带有很多卖淫活动。他们还没重新整修那个池塘，实际上它当时看上去就像一条郊区的排水沟。所以那实在算不上什么好地方。我们之所以拿到这份合同，基本上是因为没有别人来竞标。于是我们在那里开了一家高级餐厅（fine dining）。这帮我们做了平衡。那也是一门季节性很强的生意，但旺季正好和咖啡店相反。所以两者之间有很好的协同效应。此外，为了配合咖啡店生意、拓宽我们的业务范围并利用我们的一些设施，我们还开了一家宴会承办公司（catering company）和一家自动售货公司（vending company）来经营。然后纯粹是出于爱好，我在这些年里——或者说这二十来年里——投资了八九家其他的初创企业。就是朋友或熟人创业，我去投点资，或者当个合伙人什么的。但那真的只是个爱好。

turns.en: What are the difference in economics between running, you know, a bunch of student coffee shops, university coffee shops versus a fine dining restaurant like North Pond?
turns.zh: 经营一堆学生咖啡店、大学咖啡店，和经营一家像 North Pond 这样的高级餐厅，在经济账上有什么区别？

turns.en: Oh, completely different. You might as well be completely different industries too. The fine dining, a couple of things. The first, it's very chef driven. We've been there 30 years. We've had four chefs. Our newest chef just started. The last three chefs have all been on the cover of Food & Wine, won James Beard Awards, et cetera. A lot of it is sort of a celebrity chef culture. Nobody would see my picture or my name in the paper and go to the restaurant because of that. And if you look at our PR, you know, you Google me and the restaurant and you're hard-pressed to find any connection between the two. The idea was always to promote the restaurant, you know, the restaurant and the chef. The only one who was ever going to go to the restaurant because I owned it was my mom, and she already knew I owned it, so there was no sense putting that out in the PR. So it's very publicity-based, and there's a lot of sort of vagaries in the popularity of restaurants. The analogy, and knock on wood, we've been there 30 years, but in restaurants, you measure restaurant lifespans in dog years, not people years. We've been there, oh, yeah, close to 30 years, and that's so, so unusual for a restaurant. Most, particularly fine dining independent restaurants, you really have to look at them as like a Broadway play. You know, they're there for three years, and then they're gone. Every now and then there's a cat that's there for 20 years, but that is very, very unusual. Wow. So the popularity is very different. We would get a good review in Chicago Magazine and the place would be booked solid for a month. Now the coffee shop business, it's really just a matter of traffic. There's 400 students in the building on Tuesday and we get 300 visits. And there's 200 students on Friday and we get 120 visits. I mean, you can really kind of just take a look at the class schedule and I can tell you almost exactly what our sales are going to be because it's It's more of a utility where the fine dining, that's a luxury. You're going out for your birthday, you're going out for an event, whereas the coffee shops, you're going to feed yourself.
turns.zh: 哦，完全不同。你完全可以把它们当成两个截然不同的行业。高级餐厅，有几点。第一，它非常以主厨为核心。我们在那里做了 30 年，一共有过四位主厨。我们最新的主厨刚刚开始。最近三位主厨都曾登上过《食品与葡萄酒》（Food & Wine）杂志封面，拿过詹姆斯·比尔德奖（James Beard Awards）等等。这在很大程度上是一种名厨文化。没有人会因为看到我的照片或名字登在报纸上就跑去那家餐厅。如果你看我们的公关宣传，你去谷歌搜我和这家餐厅，你很难找到我们俩之间有什么关联。我们的理念一直是宣传餐厅本身，宣传餐厅和主厨。唯一会因为餐厅是我开的就去吃饭的人是我妈，而她早就知道是我开的，所以没必要把这放进公关宣传里。所以它非常依赖媒体曝光，而餐厅的人气又有很多起伏不定。这个类比是——且让我们敲敲木头讨个吉利——我们在那里做了 30 年，但在餐饮界，衡量一家餐厅的寿命要用“狗年”来算，而不是人年。我们在那里，是啊，快 30 年了，这对一家餐厅来说太不寻常了。大多数餐厅，尤其是独立的高级餐厅，你真的得把它们当成一出百老汇（Broadway）戏剧来看。它们上演个三年，然后就没了。偶尔会有一出像《猫》（Cats）那样能演 20 年的，但那非常非常罕见。哇。所以人气这件事完全不同。我们只要在《芝加哥杂志》（Chicago Magazine）上得到一篇好评，店里就会被订满整整一个月。而咖啡店生意，它真的就是客流量（traffic）的问题。周二教学楼里有 400 个学生，我们就有 300 人次光顾；周五有 200 个学生，我们就有 120 人次光顾。我的意思是，你几乎可以直接看看课表，我就能差不多准确地告诉你我们的销售额会是多少，因为它更像是一种公用事业（utility）；而高级餐厅是一种奢侈品。你是为了过生日出去吃，为了某个特别的活动出去吃；而咖啡店，你是为了填饱肚子。

turns.en: Since we talked about the difference between coffee shops in the 1980s versus the monstrosities that exist in coffee shops today, another thing that just strikes me about a fine dining restaurant that lasts as long as yours is tastes different. change and so forth, what people want. If we had the menu from the opening day versus now. What stayed the same and what's different? And how do you evolve a menu and how do you stay on trend?
turns.zh: 既然我们已经聊了 1980 年代的咖啡店和今天咖啡店里那些“怪物级”产品的区别，另一件让我印象深刻的、关于一家能像你这样长久经营的高级餐厅的事，就是口味会变，人们想要的东西会变，等等。如果我们拿开业当天的菜单和现在的菜单对比，什么没变，什么变了？你是怎么让一份菜单不断演进的，又是怎么紧跟潮流的？

turns.en: I'm trying to think of like a classic 1980s dish, like chicken marbella or something, chicken Kiev, something like that.
turns.zh: 我在努力想一道 1980 年代的经典菜，比如鸡肉马贝拉（chicken marbella）之类的，或者基辅鸡（chicken Kiev），诸如此类。

turns.en: We opened the restaurant in 1997. Okay.
turns.zh: 我们是 1997 年开的这家餐厅。好。

turns.en: So you probably had pesto. That's what I think of when I think of mid-90s food.
turns.zh: 那你们多半有青酱（pesto）。一想到 90 年代中期的食物，我脑子里浮现的就是这个。

turns.en: When we first opened it up, we were leasing the building from the Chicago Park District. Now, the Chicago Park District, their paradigm was working with concessionaires who run crappy hot dog carts that steal from us. So to go to them with this whole plan of, hey, we want to do a fine dining restaurant in the park and we want to get a liquor license, just completely over their heads. It took a total of about two and a half years just to get the permission, then about another year to build the place out. Because like I said, we had the first liquor license that was in the park. And even then, they looked at us with quite a deal of skepticism. We were not allowed to have a bar. We had to have a takeout window. I mean, things that were just absolutely incompatible with doing a fine dining restaurant. So when we first opened it up, we called it North Pond Cafe, and it was a little more casual. After a couple years with the park district, and they also had the new superintendent and the president of the park board We're two very forward-thinking individuals. And they kind of recognized what we were doing. So they gave us permission to remodel the building, add the front room, add a bar, and started treating us like a fine dining restaurant. And that was about the time our second chef started. And our second chef, absolutely brilliant young man, he had been, ironically enough, he had been a finance major at Wharton. and decided not to go into finance. Kindred spirit. Yeah. And one of the smartest, most talented chefs you're ever going to run into. And back then, we decided that the focus for the restaurant was going to be on what now we would call farm-to-table. I mean, that phrase didn't exist. I had been in California and had visited Alice Waters' restaurant. Absolutely loved the place. And it just seemed to resonate that menu and an approach to food like that in Lincoln Park, you know, just given the park-like setting. And we had built the building out. It had been a very workmanlike, just shed almost. We had built it out in the arts and craft prairie style. Seemed to be, you know, to fit with sort of our idea of the craft approach to food and also the vintage heritage and location of the building. So we really started what we call a sustainable dining, but we started what you'd call farm-to-table now. And at the time, most people didn't kind of know what to do with it. I mean, we would get our sign, the tagline in our sign was North Pond Seasonal American Dining. And we would get people that would call like, you know, oh, what season are you open? We started doing, on the menu, we started listing farmers. And people were like, who's this Mickey Klug guy? And what's a Mickey Klug pear? You know, that kind of thing. So it's actually, it's really warming to see, you know, how that whole movement has taken off.
turns.zh: 我们刚开业时，是从芝加哥公园管理局租下这栋楼的。而公园管理局，他们的思维定式是跟那些特许经营商打交道——那些人经营着劣质热狗车，还从我们这儿偷东西。所以我们拿着这么一整套计划去找他们，说：嘿，我们想在公园里开一家高级餐厅，还想拿到一张酒牌（liquor license），这完全超出了他们的理解范围。光是拿到许可就整整花了大约两年半，然后又花了大约一年才把场地建好。因为就像我说的，我们拿到的是公园里第一张酒牌。即便如此，他们还是带着相当多的怀疑看待我们。我们不被允许设一个吧台。我们必须有一个外带窗口。我是说，那些要求跟开一家高级餐厅根本水火不容。所以我们刚开业时，把它叫作 North Pond 咖啡馆（North Pond Cafe），风格更休闲一些。跟公园管理局打了几年交道后，他们也有了新的总监和公园委员会主席，这两位都是非常有前瞻性的人。他们算是认识到了我们在做的事情。于是他们批准我们改造这栋楼，加建前厅，增设吧台，并开始把我们当作一家高级餐厅来对待。那差不多正是我们第二位主厨上任的时候。我们的第二位主厨是个绝顶聪明的年轻人，讽刺的是，他曾经是沃顿商学院的金融专业学生，后来决定不进金融界。算是同道中人吧。是啊。他是你会遇到的最聪明、最有才华的主厨之一。那时我们决定，餐厅的定位将聚焦于我们现在所谓的“从农场到餐桌”（farm-to-table）。我是说，那时候这个说法还不存在。我曾去过加州，参观过爱丽丝·沃特斯（Alice Waters）的餐厅，爱死了那个地方。而那样一份菜单、那样一种对待食物的方式，放在林肯公园似乎很能引起共鸣，你知道的，就凭那种公园般的环境。而且我们把这栋楼改造好了。它原本是一栋非常朴实无华、几乎就是个棚屋的建筑。我们把它改造成了工艺美术式的草原风格（arts and craft prairie style）。这似乎，你知道的，契合我们对“匠心”式对待食物的理念，也契合这栋建筑的古朴传承和所处地段。所以我们真正开创了我们所说的“可持续餐饮”（sustainable dining），也就是你们现在会称之为“从农场到餐桌”的东西。而在当时，大多数人不太知道该怎么看待它。我是说，我们招牌上的标语是“North Pond——季节性美式餐饮”（North Pond Seasonal American Dining）。会有人打电话来问：哦，你们哪个季节营业啊？我们开始在菜单上列出供应食材的农户名字。人们就问：这个叫米基·克拉格（Mickey Klug）的家伙是谁？还有，什么叫“米基·克拉格梨”？就是这类事。所以，看到整个这场运动后来是如何兴起的，真的让人心里暖暖的。

turns.en: Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是啊。

turns.en: And at the time, I mean, our chef really embraced this, even more so than I had originally proposed, really embraced it. became very involved in this movement. He was on the, you know, the Slow Food Board. He was one of the founders of the Green City Market. Really helped because now we have a network now of close to 100 small local craft farmers and producers, you know, fishers and cheesemongers and stuff like that. And at the time, that supply network didn't exist. And these are not the 1,200 acres of corn, third-generation farmer in Iowa. This is the guy who got kicked out of the Ph.D. program at sociology department at Northwestern and now is farming organic beets in upstate Wisconsin. So it's a really interesting movement, just shift in the whole agricultural industry too. I mean, it's still a very tiny part of it, but these farmers pretty much didn't exist. And our chef, he had trained in France. So the theme originally was a very classic French preparation with this theme of sustainable dining. And he was with us for 20-something years, left, talk about, you know, good timing. He left in December of 19. And when there was one guy coughing into his egg drop soup, you know, and two months later the whole world shuts down. The third chef we hired is much more of a younger guy, much more of an international approach. And the menu for the last four or five years has been much more eclectic, much more international, and not as sort of classically French. So fine dining, but a very different take on it.
turns.zh: 而在当时，我是说，我们的主厨真的全身心拥抱了这个理念，甚至比我最初提议的还要投入，真的是全身心投入，深度参与到这场运动中。他曾在慢食运动（Slow Food）的董事会任职。他是绿色城市市集（Green City Market）的创始人之一。这真的帮了大忙，因为如今我们拥有一个由将近 100 家本地小型匠心农户和生产者组成的网络——渔民、奶酪匠等等。而在当时，那样的供应网络根本不存在。而且这些人可不是爱荷华州那种种着 1200 英亩玉米的第三代农民。这是那种被西北大学（Northwestern）社会学系博士项目踢出来、如今在威斯康星州北部种有机甜菜的人。所以这是一场非常有意思的运动，也是整个农业行业的一场转变。我是说，它仍然只是农业中很小的一部分，但这些农民过去基本上是不存在的。而我们的主厨曾在法国受训。所以最初的主题是非常经典的法式烹饪手法，配上可持续餐饮这个理念。他跟我们干了二十多年，然后离开了——说说好时机吧，他是在 2019 年 12 月离开的。那时候也就是有一个人对着他的蛋花汤咳嗽而已，两个月后全世界就停摆了。我们雇的第三位主厨是个年轻得多的人，走的是更国际化的路子。过去四五年的菜单要更加兼收并蓄、更加国际化，不再那么经典法式了。所以仍是高级餐饮，但对它的诠释非常不同。

turns.en: I'm going to ask a very direct question, but what are the profit margins actually like for a higher-end restaurant?
turns.zh: 我要问一个非常直接的问题：一家高端餐厅的利润率实际上到底是什么样？

turns.en: I think the weather's going to be really good this week.
turns.zh: 我觉得这周天气会非常好。

turns.en: No, but, like, I get these different senses. So a lot of people will say, like, oh, never start a restaurant because it never makes money. But then you see these restaurants that are incredibly popular in New York, and people are paying insane prices, and they're all full every night, and you think they must be making money.
turns.zh: 不，我是说，我会有各种不同的感觉。很多人会说：哦，千万别开餐厅，因为它根本不赚钱。可你又看到纽约那些超级火爆的餐厅，人们付着离谱的价钱，每晚都客满，你就会想：他们肯定在赚钱啊。

turns.en: Otherwise, no one would do this.
turns.zh: 要不然，就没人会干这行了。

turns.en: On an economic basis— The restaurant business is one of the worst businesses to ever get in. I mean, just the base economic, I'm talking about the independent, particularly fine dining. It's one of the worst industries to ever, ever get into. And a couple of things. The first is it's, it's hyper-competitive. There's, there's no barriers to entry. Anybody can get into it. It's also, there's a lot of entry into the restaurant business from people who don't have access, you know, talented, hardworking people. but who don't have access to the finance world or the banking world. You know, someone who's really smart, who's a first-generation immigrant, did not go to, you know, Wharton. And, you know, they're a smart, talented, hardworking guy. You can go start a restaurant. So it's very, very competitive. No barriers to entry. It's very difficult to build a moat around your business. There's nothing you can do that's proprietary. You come up with the latest croissant donut mashup.
turns.zh: 从经济角度讲——餐饮业是有史以来最糟糕的生意之一。我是说，单从基本的经济学看，我讲的是独立餐厅，尤其是高级餐厅，它是有史以来最糟糕的行业之一。有几方面。第一，它竞争极度激烈。没有进入壁垒，谁都能进来。而且，有很多人进入餐饮业是因为他们没有别的门路——你知道的，他们很有才华、很勤奋，但接触不到金融界或银行界。比如某个非常聪明的人，是个第一代移民，没上过沃顿商学院，但他聪明、有才华、肯干，他就可以去开一家餐厅。所以竞争非常非常激烈，没有进入壁垒，而且很难在你的生意周围建起一道护城河（moat）。你没有什么东西能做到专有独占。你想出了最新款的牛角甜甜圈（croissant donut）混搭……

turns.en: And everyone has it around the world.
turns.zh: 然后全世界所有人都能做出来。

turns.en: And everyone has it down. And then the last thing is that if you are intent on obeying the law, you're going to operate at a 5%, 10% deficit to all your competitors. So if you're going to pay attention to labor laws, immigration laws, overtime laws, things like that, you are operating at a serious deficit to the rest of the field. And there has been a little bit of a reckoning in the industry, but it was an industry that wage theft, overtime abuse, things like that were just absolutely rampant. There has been, if you're looking at sort of changes in this business in the last four or five years, there has been, and some of it started with sort of the Me Too movement. You talk to any woman who's ever been in the restaurant business, and I don't care whether she's front of the house, back of the house, cook, waitress, bartender, whatever. I guarantee you that if she's been in the business for six months, she's got horror stories to tell you about harassment in the industry. And that is finally, I would never say it's eliminated, but people are starting to get held to account for that. And you see a lot of high-profile chefs who are getting bounced out of their jobs. And so that's a good thing. And the same thing with the abuse of all the labor laws. And a lot of it was predicated on it was an industry that was filled with a lot of illegal immigrants. And these are people that you can abuse and not get called for it because they're not going to go to the labor board and complain. Oh, and then the final thing about why the restaurant business is tough. You never want to be in a business for economic reasons when you are competing with people who are in there for non-economic reasons. It's the same. It would be the equivalent of sports franchises. You don't spend $ 12 billion to buy the Dodgers because you think they have great cash flow. You're spending that money because you're a billionaire and you've got huge ego. And it's a game of like hot potato. In five years, you want to sell that franchise to someone else and the value has gone up. But there's a lot of people who made money in other fields. If you're a doctor and you've made millions of dollars and you're looking for something fun to do, you would never think like, oh, I'm going to go buy an auto towing business. No, because you don't know anything about toys.
turns.zh: 而且所有人都能做得出来。然后最后一点是，如果你执意守法经营，你就会比所有竞争对手多承担 5% 到 10% 的劣势。也就是说，如果你要认真对待劳动法、移民法、加班法之类的，你相较业内其他人就处于严重的劣势。这个行业已经有了一点算账清算（reckoning）的迹象，但过去这行的工资克扣（wage theft）、加班滥用之类简直是猖獗到极点。如果你看这行过去四五年的变化，确实有所改观，其中一部分是从 Me Too（#MeToo）运动开始的。你去问任何一个曾在餐饮业待过的女性，我不在乎她是前厅、后厨、厨师、服务员还是调酒师，随便什么。我敢保证，只要她在这行待过六个月，她就有一堆关于业内骚扰的可怕经历要讲给你听。而这一点终于——我绝不会说它已经被消除了——但人们开始为此被追责了。你会看到很多知名主厨被扫地出门。所以这是件好事。各种劳动法的滥用也是一样。而这很大程度上是建立在这个行业充斥着大量非法移民的基础上。这些人你可以肆意剥削却不会被追究，因为他们不会跑去劳工委员会投诉。哦，然后关于餐饮业为什么难做，还有最后一点。你永远不希望出于经济原因去做一门生意，而你的竞争对手却是出于非经济原因在做这门生意。这就跟体育球队是一个道理。你花 120 亿美元买下道奇队（Dodgers），不是因为你觉得它现金流很棒。你花那笔钱是因为你是个亿万富翁，自我意识极度膨胀。而且这就像一场“击鼓传花”（hot potato）的游戏——五年后你想把球队转手卖给别人，那时价值已经涨上去了。但有很多人是在别的领域赚到钱的。如果你是个医生，赚了几百万美元，想找点有意思的事做，你绝不会想：哦，我去买一家汽车拖吊生意吧。不会，因为你根本不懂拖吊。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: But everyone thinks that, one, just because they dine out and have preferences when they dine out, they think they can run a restaurant or start up a food business. very different. And also, people have this idea. I talk to friends, and their idea is, That I go in on Saturday night, I hang out at the bar, greet friends, buy people drinks, have a drink at the end of the bar myself, and then go home. And that's the exact opposite. Running the restaurant business is six o'clock on a Sunday morning, unclogging the drain. That's the restaurant business. So there's a lot of sort of ideas that it is somehow, you know, glamorous and cool and fun. And yeah, there can be parts to that, but that's a pretty small part of the business.
turns.zh: 但每个人都觉得，第一，仅仅因为他们经常下馆子、下馆子时有自己的偏好，就以为自己能开餐厅、能做食品生意。这完全是两回事。而且，人们还有这样一种想法。我跟朋友聊，他们的想法是：我周六晚上过去，在吧台边晃悠，跟朋友打招呼，请人喝酒，自己在吧台尽头喝一杯，然后回家。而这恰恰是相反的。经营餐厅这行是星期天早上六点去疏通下水道。那才是餐饮业。所以有很多人抱着这样的想法，觉得它不知怎么的就是光鲜、酷、有意思。是的，它可以有那样的一面，但那只是这门生意里很小的一部分。

turns.en: It's sort of the lack of everyone thinking they could run a restaurant. It's like everyone thinks they could do a podcast because they have opinions.
turns.zh: 这有点像是人人都觉得自己能开餐厅。就像人人都觉得自己能做播客，因为他们有观点。

turns.en: They're like, I have takes.
turns.zh: 他们会说：我有看法（takes）啊。

turns.en: I can do that. That's a good analogy.
turns.zh: 我也能做啊。这个类比很贴切。

turns.en: Everyone can do a podcast. It's just they might not be very good.
turns.zh: 每个人都能做播客。只是他们做的可能不太行。

turns.en: Right, right. They're like, oh, that seems easy. I can run my mouth.
turns.zh: 对对对。他们会说：哦，那看起来很容易嘛。我能耍嘴皮子啊。

turns.en: And the proof of all this is, and there's very good statistics on it. Wharton has great statistics. The SBA has great statistics. The failure rate for restaurants is abysmal. And the figures that I have seen are for the independent fine dining restaurant that as a whole, that industry has a negative return. So yes, there are people who hit it big, make lots of money. And for every rich Melman that's out there that's making boatloads of money in the restaurant business, there's 40 other guys you don't know their names because their restaurant closed and now they're back to being a dentist or whatever they did before.
turns.zh: 而这一切的证据是——这方面有非常好的统计数据。沃顿有很棒的数据，美国小企业管理局（SBA）也有很棒的数据。餐厅的失败率惨不忍睹。而我看到的那些数字显示，对独立高级餐厅整体而言，这个行业的回报是负的。所以是的，有人一夜爆红、赚得盆满钵满。但对于每一个在餐饮业赚得盆满钵满的里奇·梅尔曼（Rich Melman）式人物，就有另外 40 个你根本不知道名字的人，因为他们的餐厅关门了，如今又回去当牙医或者干回他们之前的老本行了。

turns.en: So without going into exactly what your profit margins are. But like, maybe you could talk about like theory of menu design. Cause there are, there are these things that people say, Oh, you only make your money on wine or something like that. What is like this sort of like you construct a menu. What are the principles of menu constructing and where do the profits come from on that menu?
turns.zh: 那么，在不具体谈你的利润率到底是多少的前提下，也许你可以聊聊菜单设计的理论。因为人们会说：哦，你只在葡萄酒上赚钱之类的。你是怎么设计一份菜单的？菜单设计有哪些原则？那份菜单上的利润来自哪里？

turns.en: Well, a step back just one second is the profit margin for restaurants is post-pandemic, it's probably seriously negative. You know, you had three years where pretty much everybody lost money and even the recovery hasn't been very good. But in terms of profitability, menu mix and things like that, there's one of the biggest sea changes in the last like 23, 20, 30 years is happening right now. And your statement about restaurants making money on wine is absolutely true. We do a prefix menu and it's $ 130, five courses, And I've got, on a Saturday night, I've got nine to ten guys in the kitchen in the pastry department who are preparing that meal. And we've got waiters, back waiters, and busboys, you know, serving the table. And that's for that $ 130 dinner. If you're sitting at that dinner, now you order, our average bottle of wine is about $ 110. You order a bottle of wine from us, it takes the waiter two minutes to walk over to the wine cellar, bring it back, open it. and put it on your table. And the profitability margin on that wine is about the same as the food with almost none of the associated costs. Now, the thing that is kind of got every restaurateur nervous as hell, and I'll use our figures as an example. We've been in business almost 30 years. For the first 28 years, our liquor wine sales, and we're almost exclusively wine, our wine sales were just a hair over 33%. So between 33 to 34% every year, like clockwork. In the last 18 months, that has dropped to 24%. That is a huge deal because that 8% was the most profitable sales that we did. And people just are not drinking like they used to, particularly our younger guests.
turns.zh: 那么，先退一步说，餐厅的利润率在疫情后很可能是严重为负的。你知道的，有那么三年几乎人人都在亏钱，就连复苏也不怎么好。但就盈利能力、菜单结构等而言，过去二三十年里最大的巨变之一正在此刻发生。你说的“餐厅靠葡萄酒赚钱”这句话千真万确。我们做的是固定价格套餐（prix fixe），130 美元，五道菜。周六晚上，我在厨房和甜点部门有九到十个人在准备这顿饭，还有服务员、副服务员和传菜员在上菜。而这就是那份 130 美元的晚餐。如果你坐在那顿晚餐里，现在你点酒，我们平均每瓶葡萄酒大约 110 美元。你从我们这里点一瓶酒，服务员只需花两分钟走到酒窖，把酒取回来，开瓶，放到你桌上。而那瓶酒的利润率跟食物差不多，却几乎没有相应的成本。现在，有件事让每一位餐饮业老板都紧张得要命——我用我们自己的数据举个例子。我们营业快 30 年了。在头 28 年里，我们的酒水（我们几乎全是葡萄酒）销售占比每年都刚好略高于 33%，就在 33% 到 34% 之间，像时钟一样精准。而在过去 18 个月里，这个比例已经跌到了 24%。这是件大事，因为那 8% 是我们所做的一切销售里利润最高的部分。而人们就是不像过去那样喝酒了，尤其是我们更年轻的客人。

turns.en: I was going to ask, is this the generational.
turns.zh: 我正想问，这是不是我们常听到的那种世代……

turns.en: Shift that we hear about? I mean, some of it is just people, you know, for health, they're not drinking. A lot of it also is that people are, you know, there's an entire industry, you know, the cannabis CBD industry out there. And you're just starting to see that work into menus with Lollapalooza this year for the first year had THC margaritas. So you're starting to see, you know, things like this show up on menus. We've got a proposal with the Park District to add them to our menu. We haven't been approved for it yet. We just put in a non-alcoholic cocktail menu. But the fact that people aren't drinking is a really big problem for most restaurants.
turns.zh: ……转变？我是说，一部分原因就是人们，你懂的，出于健康考虑不喝酒了。很大一部分还在于，人们……你懂的，外面有一整个大麻、CBD 产业。而你才刚刚开始看到它进入菜单。今年的 Lollapalooza 音乐节第一次有了含 THC 的玛格丽特鸡尾酒。所以你开始看到这类东西出现在菜单上。我们向公园管理局提交了一份申请，想把它们加到我们的菜单上。我们还没获批。我们刚刚上线了一份无酒精鸡尾酒菜单。但人们不喝酒这个事实，对大多数餐厅来说是一个非常大的问题。

turns.en: Do you see any impact from GLP-1s?
turns.zh: 你有没有看到 GLP-1（一类减肥药物）带来的影响？

turns.en: Not specifically because it's hard to identify that versus more global, other sort of megatrends. I'm sure it is affecting. I mean, what is it, like 20% of the country is on GLP? I don't remember the number now, but it's a pretty significant amount. And I just can't imagine that you're on a GLP and you want to come in and have five courses and then finish that with these incredible desserts we make and then also have a glass of port. It seems a little incongruous.
turns.zh: 没有特别明显的，因为很难把它和其他更全局性的大趋势区分开来。我确信它确实在产生影响。我是说，这国家大概有 20% 的人在用 GLP-1 吧？我记不清具体数字了，但那是相当大的比例。我就是没法想象，一个正在用 GLP-1 的人会想进来吃五道菜，然后再用我们做的这些不可思议的甜点收尾，接着还来一杯波特酒（port）。这似乎有点自相矛盾。

turns.en: Maybe there's still room for a CBD-infused pastry of some sort. I'd be interested.
turns.zh: 也许某种注入了 CBD 的糕点还是有市场的。我会感兴趣。

turns.en: Well, the THC infused.
turns.zh: 嗯，那些注入了 THC 的……

turns.en: Margaritas, yeah.
turns.zh: ……玛格丽特，对。

turns.en: Well, that gets people eating more.
turns.zh: 嗯，那玩意儿会让人吃得更多。

turns.en: Yeah, that's true.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。

turns.en: So that might create a positive flywheel.
turns.zh: 所以那也许能形成一个正向的飞轮（flywheel）。

turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: It's October 2026 right now. What do you give us like a little snapshot of what you're seeing in terms of labor availability, food costs, like the sort of like basic like economic measures that would go into it?
turns.zh: 现在是 2026 年 10 月。你能不能给我们大致描述一下你目前所看到的状况，比如劳动力的可得性、食品成本，也就是这门生意所需的那些基本经济指标？

turns.en: The restaurant business and those two particular items have been hit with inflation and scarcity. probably more than any other industry. Labor has gotten crazy. We pay about 30% more for starting cooks than we did three, four years ago. And food costs have just gone through the roof. It's one of the highest inflation sectors in the economy. Although we have not had as much of an effect as some other restaurants have had because we have a whole network of of suppliers and farmers that to some extent are isolated from the global economy. So when we're dealing with Joe's Organic Artichokes from Wisconsin, this man's, his cost basis is not being affected by tariffs or. Straight or Hormuz. Yeah, straight or Hormuz, or generally, you know, not as affected by things like diesel costs and things like that. But the inflation in this industry has been incredible. And there's no sort of lag between our sales and our costs. Everything that we put on the plate, we bought that week. So when there's inflation, we see it immediately. We've raised prices four times in the last two years, about every six months, which we used to sort of balance it out and do it once a year, unless there was a specific item that might have particularly whined that was on allocation or something like that. But generally, the prices would, once a year, we'd review it. And 1%, 2% inflation economy, that's not a big deal. But when you have a 3%, 3.5% inflation, and then 7% inflation in the food business, you really had to stay on top of that. And it's tough. I mean, going out, if you and your partner come out to North Pond for dinner and you have the wine pairing, It's going to be $ 400 for the two of you. And you have to do a lot to justify someone to spend $ 400 with you. So it really has forced us to kind of up our game in terms of the things that we do and how we treat our guests. And what it has become is, you know, people don't dine at North Pond because they're hungry. They dine because they want the experience. But we have seen a little bit of a trend where we're getting more and a higher percentage of our guests are coming in for very special events in their lives, the 25th anniversary, the 50th birthday, the graduated from college, that kind of thing. We don't get as many, hey, it's Thursday night, let's treat ourselves to a really nice meal. It's becoming much more of an event.
turns.zh: 餐饮业，尤其是那两个特定项目（劳动力和食品），受到通胀和稀缺的冲击，可能比任何其他行业都严重。劳动力成本已经涨疯了。我们付给初级厨师的薪水比三四年前高了大约 30%。而食品成本更是一飞冲天。它是经济中通胀最高的板块之一。不过，我们受到的影响没有其他一些餐厅那么大，因为我们有一整张供应商和农户的网络，他们在一定程度上是与全球经济隔绝的。所以当我们在跟“威斯康星州乔氏有机朝鲜蓟”（Joe's Organic Artichokes）打交道时，这个人的成本基础不会受到关税的影响，也不会受到霍尔木兹海峡（Strait of Hormuz）的影响。是啊，霍尔木兹海峡，或者总体上也不太受柴油成本之类的影响。但这个行业的通胀确实令人难以置信。而且我们的销售额和成本之间没有任何滞后。我们放到盘子上的每一样东西，都是那一周买的。所以一旦有通胀，我们立刻就感受到了。过去两年里我们涨了四次价，大约每六个月一次；而过去我们通常是一年调一次价来平衡，除非某样特定食材——比如某种被配额供应、价格叫得特别高的东西。但总体上，价格我们一年审视一次。在 1%、2% 通胀的经济里，那不算什么大事。但当你面对 3%、3.5% 的通胀，然后食品行业又是 7% 的通胀时，你就真的得盯紧它了。而这很难。我是说，出去吃一顿——如果你和你的伴侣来 North Pond 吃晚餐，还点了葡萄酒配餐（wine pairing），那两个人就要 400 美元。而你要做很多工作，才能让人觉得花 400 美元在你这儿是值得的。所以这真的逼着我们在所做的每件事、以及我们对待客人的方式上都提升水准。而它现在变成的是——人们来 North Pond 吃饭不是因为饿了。他们来吃饭是想要那种体验。但我们确实看到一个趋势：越来越多、比例越来越高的客人是为了人生中非常特别的事件而来——结婚 25 周年纪念、50 岁生日、大学毕业之类。我们不太会再有那种“嘿，周四晚上，咱们犒劳自己吃顿好的”的客人。它正越来越变成一种“事件”。

turns.en: So I wanted to ask about your other venture now, which is the Spark Shared Kitchen. What's the difference between a shared kitchen and a ghost kitchen?
turns.zh: 那我想问问你现在的另一项事业，也就是 Spark 共享厨房。共享厨房（shared kitchen）和幽灵厨房（ghost kitchen）有什么区别？

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: Is this rebranding?
turns.zh: 这是重新包装（rebranding）吗？

turns.en: It's some subtle changes. The similarity is that they're both kitchen facilities that are used by multiple vendors and typically owned by a third party. Ghost kitchens are typically thought of as someone has a brand, whether it's Popeye's Chicken or Joe's Italian Subs, and you open a small takeout-only location and it's in a central facility. It's all set up for very easy delivery to the DoorDashes and the Uber Eats of the world. So it's really for... food delivery companies. Now the shared kitchen model is a little different. In there, we build out kitchens that people can use for food businesses. The biggest use of them we have is by caterers. So you have a small catering company, you can come in and you can run a kitchen. And we have two types of rentals too. We have a couple fully equipped kitchens you can come in and rent by the hour. So if you have a You know, you have Tracy's granola and.
turns.zh: 有一些细微的差别。它们的相似之处在于，两者都是供多个经营者使用、通常由第三方拥有的厨房设施。幽灵厨房通常被理解为：某人有一个品牌，不管是 Popeyes 炸鸡还是“乔氏意大利三明治”，然后你开一个小型的、只做外带的门店，设在一个集中的设施里，一切都为非常方便地配送到 DoorDash、Uber Eats 这些平台上而设置好。所以它其实是面向……食品配送公司的。而共享厨房模式则有点不同。在那里，我们建造可供人们用于食品生意的厨房。我们最大的用途是宴会承办商。也就是说，如果你有一家小型的宴会承办公司，你可以进来，运营一个厨房。我们还有两种出租方式。我们有几间设备齐全的厨房，你可以按小时租进来。所以如果你有——你知道的，你有“崔西牌格兰诺拉麦片”（Tracy's granola），然后……

turns.en: No, not granola. It'd be something else.
turns.zh: 不，不会是格兰诺拉麦片。会是别的东西。

turns.en: What would you make?
turns.zh: 那你会做什么？

turns.en: What would be your thing, Tracy?
turns.zh: 崔西，你的招牌会是什么？

turns.en: you rent our kitchen. You only need a kitchen maybe five hours a week. You come in, you rent our kitchen, you make your production, you can rent some storage space to us, but you're only paying us for those five hours. We also have kitchens where you can come in and you can rent this kitchen and And we've got some small ones that are 400 feet and they go up to 1,600 feet. You can rent that kitchen. You have access to it 24-7. You've got your own key. Everything in there is yours. And we provide you with a kitchen. And the kitchen has the very basics, the hood, the sinks, the flooring, the floor drains, all that stuff. You just have to bring in all your equipment. Now, the advantage of that is if you were to go out and licensed facility. And, you know, you could spend months looking for that. Landlords typically want a three to five year minimum rent. Then you're going to have to put a deposit down. You're going to have to go through the whole licensing process. Minimum, it's going to take you six months to do it. The great thing about shared kitchens is you can come in and you can open basically for the price of your ingredients and the license. And the license, you can go down to City Hall, you get a shared kitchen user license, and you get that on Monday and you can come Because we have a shared kitchen operator license. You get the license on Monday and on Tuesday you can be in business. So it is a great way to encourage entrepreneurship. It's one of the better things that Citi has done over the last like five, ten years.
turns.zh: ……你就来租我们的厨房。你也许一周只需要用五个小时厨房。你进来，租我们的厨房，做你的生产，你可以向我们租一些仓储空间，但你只为那五个小时付费。我们还有一些厨房，你可以进来把这间厨房租下来。我们有一些小的，400 平方英尺，一直到大到 1600 平方英尺。你可以租下那间厨房。你可以全天候 24 小时进出，你有自己的钥匙，里面的一切都是你的。而我们为你提供一个厨房。这个厨房配备最基本的东西——排烟罩、水槽、地板、地漏，所有这些。你只需要把自己的设备搬进来。这样做的好处是：如果你要自己出去租一个持牌合规的设施，你可能得花好几个月去找。房东通常要求至少三到五年的租期。然后你还得交押金，还得走完整个申领执照的流程。最少也得花你六个月才能搞定。而共享厨房最棒的地方在于，你进来后基本上只要花食材和执照的钱就能开业。至于执照，你可以去市政厅（City Hall），领一张“共享厨房用户执照”（shared kitchen user license），周一拿到，周二你就能开张营业——因为我们持有一张“共享厨房运营方执照”（shared kitchen operator license）。所以你周一拿到执照，周二就能开业。因此它是鼓励创业的一种绝佳方式。这是芝加哥市过去五到十年里做得比较好的事情之一。

turns.en: You know what it reminds me of, Tracy? The shared child care space in Mount Airy.
turns.zh: 你知道这让我想起了什么吗，崔西？就是芒特埃里（Mount Airy）那个共享的托儿空间。

turns.en: Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，对。

turns.en: Because if you think of, like, a child care entrepreneur and, like, okay, they want to take care of children, but do they want to spend their time thinking about, you know, licensing and, like, the building codes, et cetera. So let another entity just sort of do all this sort of blocking and tackling with, like, all of that and then just, like, do the actual business that you, like, So talk to us a little bit of, I guess, like the economics of that business or like scaling that up or how easy has it been to get tenants into the kitchen?
turns.zh: 因为如果你想一想，比如一个托儿创业者，好，他们想照顾孩子，但他们愿意把时间花在琢磨——你知道的——申领执照、建筑规范等等这些事上吗？所以让另一个实体去替你把所有这些脏活累活都干了，然后你就去做你真正想做的那门生意就好。那么跟我们讲讲，我想，这门生意的经济账，或者把它规模化，或者说把租户招进厨房到底有多容易？

turns.en: It has been very easy getting tenants. The biggest problem with it, it's a very capital intensive business. Building restaurant kitchens, short of building hospital rooms, they're about the most expensive on a square foot basis thing you can do. But the economics are so compelling on the other end. I'll give you one example. We have a small 800-square-foot facility, and we just got it licensed. And it doesn't have a hood on it. It was made for– I had three people approach me. They were going to start ice cream businesses. We went out, built this facility out. And, again, it doesn't have a hood, so it wasn't as expensive as most kitchens. And we just ordered a $ 26, 000 five-gallon industrial ice cream machine for it. Now, these people who are doing it, one's doing a specialty Hispanic-themed ice cream, another's doing one with Asian-flavored ice creams. You can come in in a day and you can make 200 gallons of ice cream, put them in the deep freeze, plus your ingredients. You spend $ 1, 000 with us or something along those lines. where it would be almost impossible to do that on your own without a complete facility. And you'd have to go buy that $ 20, 000 ice cream machine, or you'd buy a $ 5, 000 ice cream machine that has one gallon capacity and you can make 10 gallons in a day versus making 50 or 100 gallons in a day. So the economics are very compelling. Anytime you've got a lot of capital costs involved, and an individual would use them, you know, two, four, six, eight hours a week. And you can get the scale of having three, four, whatever number of people using them. It's incredibly efficient. And all the associated costs with it, the licensing, the, you know, the property taxes, the search costs to find a facility. So the shared kitchens are It's a great little engine for the city's economy.
turns.zh: 招租户一直非常容易。它最大的问题在于，这是一门非常资本密集的生意。建造餐厅厨房——除了建医院病房之外——按每平方英尺算，它差不多是你能做的最贵的东西了。但另一端的经济账实在太有说服力了。我给你举一个例子。我们有一处 800 平方英尺的小设施，我们刚刚给它拿到了执照。它没有装排烟罩。它是为——有三个人来找我，他们打算开冰淇淋生意。我们就出去建了这处设施。同样，它没有排烟罩，所以不像大多数厨房那么贵。我们刚为它订购了一台价值 26000 美元、五加仑容量的工业级冰淇淋机。现在，这些来做冰淇淋的人，一个做的是西语裔主题的特色冰淇淋，另一个做的是亚洲风味的冰淇淋。你进来一天就能做出 200 加仑冰淇淋，把它们放进冷冻库，加上你的食材，你在我们这儿花个 1000 美元左右或类似的数目。而如果完全没有这样一处设施，你自己几乎不可能做到这一点。你得去买那台两万美元的冰淇淋机，或者你买一台五千美元、只有一加仑容量的冰淇淋机，一天只能做 10 加仑，而不是一天做 50 或 100 加仑。所以这经济账非常有说服力。任何时候，只要涉及大量资本成本，而单个用户一周只用上两小时、四小时、六小时、八小时，你就能通过让三个人、四个人、随便多少人共同使用来获得规模效应。这效率极高。而且所有相关成本——执照、房产税、找场地的搜寻成本——都被摊薄了。所以共享厨房对这座城市经济来说，是一个很棒的“小引擎”。

turns.en: Just real quickly, could they theoretically be used as ghost kitchens?
turns.zh: 就很快问一下，理论上它们能被用作幽灵厨房吗？

turns.en: Oh, yeah, absolutely. Absolutely. The other difference between ghost and shared kitchens, ghost kitchens typically tend to be smaller and in much more desirable real estate because they need to be within five. Like there's one, I live in the South Loop. There's one about three minutes south of us, 22nd and 22nd. and Wabash. Now they can get to the whole South Loop in, you know, in five minutes. And there's 80,000 people living in the South Loop. Our facility is in Brighton Park. It's a 60,000 square foot warehouse. And we're, you know, two thirds of the way to Midway Airport. And unless you were on the way to the, got lost on the way to the airport, you'd never realize. We're an industrial area. You could never run a ghost kitchen. There's just not the density of apartments and residents. So that's, that's another one, just the location. Our building is, on a square foot basis, is probably a third of the value of what their buildings are.
turns.zh: 哦，能，绝对能。绝对能。幽灵厨房和共享厨房的另一个区别是，幽灵厨房通常倾向于更小、位于更抢手的地段，因为它们需要在五分钟车程内。比如有一家，我住在南环区（South Loop），有一家就在我们南边大约三分钟的地方，在 22 街和瓦巴什大道（Wabash）那里。这样他们就能在五分钟内到达整个南环区。而南环区住着八万人。我们的设施在布莱顿公园（Brighton Park），是一栋六万平方英尺的仓库。我们大概在去中途机场（Midway Airport）路程三分之二的地方。除非你是在去机场的路上、或者去机场时迷了路，否则你根本不会注意到我们。我们是一个工业区。你在那儿永远没法经营幽灵厨房，因为那里根本没有足够密集的公寓和居民。所以那又是一个区别，就是选址。我们这栋楼按每平方英尺算，价值大概只有他们那些楼的三分之一。

turns.en: You mentioned licensing for the shared kitchen. And I feel like whenever we talk to restauranteurs, dealing with the city and regulations always seems to be some form of complaint. Has it changed over the— Yeah, trauma. Shared trauma. Has it changed over the years? Has it gotten better, the sort of red tape issue?
turns.zh: 你提到了共享厨房的执照问题。我感觉每次我们跟餐饮业者聊天，跟市政府和监管打交道似乎总会以某种形式变成吐槽。这些年有变化吗——是的，创伤。共同的创伤。这些年它有变化吗？那种繁文缛节（red tape）的问题有没有变好一些？

turns.en: Absolutely. Okay. I noticed some real changes when Rahm was mayor. I mean, the joke was that eighth floor, which is where all the licensing is, eighth floor was the department of no. I mean, they would just go out of their way to find reasons to tell you no. And it was just an ungodly, burdensome task getting a license. It is much, much better now, but it is still not a real efficient process. So it went from a D minus, now it's a B minus. But generally, when you go to City Hall now, they are trying to help you open that business. So there's still a lot of little vagaries in the licensing and things like that. But the tone when you talk to people and you work with them, they're generally much more supportive. And they are trying to get your business open.
turns.zh: 有，绝对的。好。我在拉姆（Rahm，即前市长拉姆·伊曼纽尔 Rahm Emanuel）当市长时注意到一些实实在在的变化。我是说，那时的笑话是：八楼——也就是所有执照审批所在的地方——八楼就是那个“专说不”的部门。我是说，他们会千方百计地找理由拒绝你。而且办一张执照是一项极其要命、负担沉重的苦差事。现在好多了，但它仍然算不上一个真正高效的流程。所以它从一个 D-（成绩）变成了现在的 B-。但总体上，现在你去市政厅，他们是在努力帮你把生意开起来。所以在执照等方面仍然有很多细小的不确定性。但当你跟人交谈、跟他们打交道时的那种态度，他们通常要支持得多。而且他们是在努力让你的生意开起来。

turns.en: All right, Richard, thank you so much for coming on All Thoughts. Really appreciate getting your perspective.
turns.zh: 好的，理查德，非常感谢你来做客《Odd Lots》。真的很感激能听到你的见解。

turns.en: Oh, glad to be here. Glad it was very enjoyable. Thank you.
turns.zh: 哦，很高兴来到这里。很高兴，非常愉快。谢谢。

turns.en: Joe, that was really enjoyable.
turns.zh: 乔，那期真的很精彩。

turns.en: That was so fun.
turns.zh: 太有意思了。

turns.en: I thought the comments about restaurants being a competitive industry, I mean, kind of obvious, but this idea that it's very hard to draw a moat around your business, especially when popularity tends to be fleeting for a lot of the new hotspots, right?
turns.zh: 我觉得那些关于餐饮业是个竞争激烈的行业的评论，我是说，虽然有点显而易见，但“很难在你的生意周围挖出一道护城河”这个观点——尤其是对很多新晋网红店来说人气往往转瞬即逝——对吧？

turns.en: Yeah, and the fact, and I guess it's obvious, but I hadn't thought of it, that there are just a lot of people in it, I guess, quote, for the love of the game, unquote, who are.
turns.zh: 是啊，而且这个事实——我想它虽然显而易见，但我之前没想过——就是这行里有很多人，我想，是“出于对这门生意的热爱”而进来的，他们并不是……

turns.en: Not in it because.
turns.zh: ……并不是因为（赚钱）才干这行的。

turns.en: So you're not competing in the same game, right? Because they don't care about making money.
turns.zh: 所以你其实并不是在同一场游戏里竞争，对吧？因为他们根本不在乎赚不赚钱。

turns.en: Yes, you figure like some, you know, athlete or something like that, for example, and people want to have their, it's kind of like their clubhouse or something like that, or some of these vanity endeavors where it's like, oh, I'm okay losing money. That's really hard to compete against.
turns.zh: 是啊，你想，比如某个运动员之类的，人们想拥有他们的——这有点像他们的俱乐部会所之类的，或者是某些虚荣性的项目，就是那种：哦，我亏钱也无所谓。这真的很难与之竞争。

turns.en: And then, of course... The idea.
turns.zh: 然后，当然了……还有那个观点——

turns.en: That it's hard to be competitive if you want to follow the law, which I think is a really big deal. And the fact that if you're serious about immigration law and all these things and proper overtime and all of these things, that if you take these seriously, if you want to do it well, you're really worsening your economics.
turns.zh: ——就是说如果你想守法就很难有竞争力，我觉得这是件非常了不起、非常重要的大事。而且，如果你认真对待移民法、认真对待正当加班等等所有这些事，如果你把这些当真，如果你想把这门生意做好，你就真的在恶化你自己的经济账。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: Also.
turns.zh: 而且。

turns.en: The shared kitchen idea is an interesting one because you basically I guess you pool together all the capital for that initial investment and the cost of the lease and stuff like that. And then everyone can benefit from it rather than having to go out and purchase their own kitchen. Like you said, it's very similar to the Mount Airy example.
turns.zh: 共享厨房这个点子很有意思，因为基本上，我想，你把那笔初始投资、租约成本等等所有的资本都汇集到了一起，然后每个人都能从中受益，而不必自己出去买一个厨房。就像你说的，这跟芒特埃里那个例子非常相似。

turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.en: source of great drama in our community.
turns.zh: （那可是）我们社区里一大出好戏的来源。

turns.en: you want to spend your time... on random things like licenses and the health inspectors and all that stuff that has nothing to do with whether your.
turns.zh: 你并不想把时间花在……各种杂乱的事情上，比如执照、卫生检查员，以及所有那些跟你（生意好不好）其实毫无关系的事情上。

turns.en: For real.
turns.zh: 真的。

turns.en: No, I think those types of businesses where you like identify, I mean.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得那类生意，你去识别出，我是说……

turns.en: Some common constraint.
turns.zh: ……某种共同的约束。

turns.en: The other thing is like to Richard's point earlier about, you know, like a Wharton grad versus a non-Wharton grad, one person's competitive advantage might be they're just a really good chef or they just have a really good feel for flavors and actually they suck at maybe identifying residential real estate, signing leases, sourcing capital, and all those other things. They suck at Excel, basically. And so if you can divide some of that up, it seems like an interesting proposition.
turns.zh: 另一点是，就像理查德先前说的那个观点，你知道的，比如一个沃顿毕业生对比一个非沃顿毕业生——一个人的竞争优势可能就是他是个非常出色的厨师，或者他就是对风味有非常好的感觉，但实际上他也许很不擅长识别住宅类房产、签租约、寻找资本，以及所有那些其他事情。他基本上就是不擅长 Excel。所以如果你能把其中一部分工作分担出去，这似乎是个很有意思的命题。
